# The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence: Five Criteria for Choosing Special Strength Exercises

**What it is** — The authors open section 4.3 by arguing that "All sporting movement is specific and goal-directed," so the strength shown in each movement is also specific, and "One should not refer to strength in general, but only in the context of the given task." The means and methods of strength training should therefore give "an adequate conditioning regime for the motor system in the special exercises." The foundation is the principle of dynamic correspondence: training means for a given sport should be chosen to enhance the required motor qualities in terms of five criteria (PDF p. 252 / printed p. 241):
1. the amplitude and direction of movement (4.3.1);
2. the accentuated region of force production (4.3.2);
3. the dynamics of the effort (4.3.3);
4. the rate and time of maximum force production (4.3.4);
5. the regime of muscular work (4.3.5).

Section 4.3.6 closes the set by stating that the character of muscular work is learned from analysis of the athlete's movements, and that "success in selecting the means of special strength training is determined by a thorough knowledge of the biomechanics of the movements" (PDF p. 259 / printed p. 248).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is the specificity argument above: strength is always expressed in a particular task, so a training means only transfers to the extent that it reproduces the task's conditions on these five dimensions. They do not give a physiological mechanism for transfer in this section; each sub-criterion gives its own reasoning (see Related). Inference: the five criteria read as the exercise-selection version of the broader specificity dimensions the book lists in 1.4, narrowed to features a coach can inspect in a movement.

**When to apply** — Use the five criteria as a checklist when choosing or designing a special strength exercise for a sport skill: check each criterion in turn rather than judging transfer by whether the exercise "looks like" the sport. Eric's baseline: "The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky), matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill, governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport." Tagged **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 103). Inference: this entry is the primary-source version of the list Eric already teaches in HHPR 5355, so it can be cited directly for the criteria's original wording.

**When NOT to apply** — The criteria select special strength exercises; the authors say in the opening of the next chapter that this selection is "only part of the process" and that methods are a separate task (cross-reference only, PDF p. 266 / printed p. 255). They are not an argument against general preparation: the text gives no rule here for how much general work an athlete needs. The authors offer the criteria as reasoned principles with illustrative examples, not as the result of controlled transfer studies, so a high correspondence score does not by itself prove that an exercise will transfer. The text gives no ranking among the criteria. The authors say that following the amplitude and direction requirements "can sometimes lead to such initial positions using weights or pulley machines which are incongruous and artificial (Fig 4.22)," but that "this occurs only when an exercise is attempted which fails to take into consideration the appropriate criteria," and they add that the Fig 4.22 exercise "may be appropriate if applied carefully" (PDF p. 256 / printed p. 245). So they do not treat the criteria as conflicting. Inference: in practice, meeting all five at once may still force a compromise; the book does not address that case.

**Example** — The authors' own examples for each criterion: the rower and shot putter whose shoulder movements have similar amplitude but opposite force direction (Fig 4.17, PDF p. 253 / printed p. 242); the standing hip-flexor machine that misses the sprinter's range (PDF p. 253 / printed p. 242); the boxer and shot putter who should do the same pulley thrust with different loads and tempos (PDF p. 258 / printed p. 247).

=========== heuristic--rfd-as-correspondence-criterion-and-impulse-cannot-compare-movements
# Use the Rate of Force Development as a Correspondence Criterion; Do Not Use Impulse to Compare Different Movements

**What it is** — The criterion of correspondence for "the rate of developing maximum force" complements the dynamic-effort criterion and "is particularly important in those sporting activities requiring explosive strength" (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246). "The ability to increase power or explosive strength also depends on specifically training the RFD factor," which the authors call "vital" to programme design for any sport with explosive actions, and they name plyometric training as "one of the practical consequences" of this analysis. Explosive strength may be evaluated by power, impulse (F.Δt) or the Reactivity Coefficient (RC = Fmax/tmax.mg = RFDmax/W), "although the significance of each of them can be different": impulse "is acceptable only when it is not necessary to compare different movements"; comparing movements would be valid "only if the time taken is identical for each movement, a situation that does not occur in human movement," so for that purpose "determination of the impulse of the force is irrelevant" (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246). Where effort lasts only briefly, "if it is necessary for the athlete to produce a large force within some time limit, he must do it quickly and use a high RFD," a necessity set by the activity and "especially the working amplitude of the movement." RFD "is an important criterion of correspondence ... which relates directly to the characteristics of the neuromuscular system," and "all training is primarily neuromuscular and ... training based entirely on variables such as exercise choice, load, sets and repetitions is highly inadequate for producing sport specific fitness" (PDF p. 258 / printed p. 247).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: when the time available is limited by the movement's amplitude, how fast force rises decides how much force can be applied; and impulse depends on duration, so two movements of different duration cannot be compared on it. They tie RFD to "the characteristics of the neuromuscular system" without further mechanism here.

**When to apply** — When an action has a short force-application window (jumps, sprints, throws, blocking contact): pick exercises and tests that reproduce the rate of force rise, not just peak force; use RFD or RC rather than impulse when comparing different exercises or tests. Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ testing is the daily readiness marker [**Explicit**, `docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74], and the CMJ family is run on ForceDecks [**Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)**, line 77]. Inference: mRSI is a time-normalised jump index, so it fits this criterion's preference for rate over impulse; the book does not discuss mRSI.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors' rejection of impulse is scoped to comparing different movements; they accept it within one movement. Their statement that training built only on exercise choice, load, sets and repetitions is "highly inadequate" is a strong judgment without cited data. The RC formula repeats the 2.2.1 definition; the book defines RC in more than one way elsewhere (see [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]), so check which form a source means.

**Example** — The book's own: plyometric training as the practical consequence of treating RFD as a trainable factor (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246).

**Related** — [[claim--average-or-peak-force-times-velocity-is-not-power]], [[principle--training-effort-must-match-or-exceed-sport-effort-judged-by-movement-speed]], [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]], [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]], [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]], [[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/framework--explosive-strength-deficit-and-rate-of-force-development-indices]].
=========== claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max
# The Authors Locate Endurance in the Muscles' Oxidative and Strength Qualities Rather Than in VO2 Max, but Give Conflicting Advice on Glycolytic Work

**What it is** — Under "Oxidative Capacity and Muscular Endurance" (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249, verified against the page image), the authors cite research that endurance gains are "associated more with enhancing the ability of the muscles to utilise a higher percentage of the oxygen already in the blood than with increasing the amount of oxygen in the bloodstream" (Ekblom 1969; Rowell 1971; Saltin 1974). "A rise in intramuscular energy potential, the power of the oxidative processes and the contractile (strength) qualities of the muscles decrease the rate of glycolysis" (four citations), and lactate falls "in the skeletal muscles and not in the liver and myocardium, as has always been believed" (Jorfeldt 1970; Knutten 1971; Gollnick & Hermansen 1973). Their italicised conclusion: "the development of endurance is associated with functional specialisation of the skeletal muscles, particularly the enhancement of their strength and oxidative qualities, rather than improvement of cardiorespiratory ability." So the emphasis should be "to decrease the proportion of glycolysis in supplying the energy for work and improve the ability of the muscles to oxidise lactate during work, and not simply to improve accommodation to high concentrations of blood lactate," aiming "chiefly at eliminating the disparity between the anaerobic and aerobic abilities of the muscles."

**Why it works** — The mechanism the authors give: stronger, more oxidative muscle relies less on glycolysis, makes less lactate and oxidises more of it in the muscle itself. They support it with citations, not with data shown in the text.

**When to apply** — When planning endurance or repeat-effort conditioning: include strength work and work that develops the working muscles' oxidative capacity, not only central (heart-lung) work. Eric's baseline: "Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress." **Explicit** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 124). Eric's baseline: for football, glycolytic conditioning is a "worst case scenario" absorbed through camp and practice [**Explicit**, line 116], though "our staff does program it in the off-season" [**Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)**, line 117]. Inference: the authors' "decrease the proportion of glycolysis" line supports the first; their own p.249 and p.253 statements (below) support the off-season glycolytic work.

**When NOT to apply** — Why `contested`: the authors' own pages pull in opposite directions.
- Raise VO2 max, or not: "Since OBLA depends on VO2 max, it is considered useful to strive to raise VO2 max, and in particular, to create some reserve of aerobic power by the end of the preparatory period" (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249), against "effectiveness of training does not lie in raising VO2 max, but in enhancing the haemodynamic efficiency of oxygen transport" (PDF p. 261 / printed p. 250).
- Glycolytic work, more or less: "it is advisable to execute a specific part of the training load with a high blood lactate concentration" (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249) and, for skaters, "it [is] necessary to have excellent movement technique and a high level of anaerobic (non-oxidative glycolytic) productivity" (PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253), against "decrease the proportion of glycolysis" (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249).

Inference: the passages may describe different aims (a VO2 max reserve before the season; muscle-level economy as the main target), but the text does not reconcile them. Also unclear on the same page: "Anaerobic work is approximately 50% more effective than aerobic work in raising this lactate threshold, therefore it is to the athlete's advantage to execute prolonged, intense work without the preliminary accumulation of lactate and include anaerobic energy production (Christensen & Hogberg, 1950)" (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249); the "therefore" does not follow clearly from the 50% figure, and no measure of "effective" is given. The sources are 1950-1975 and are not described.

**Example** — The book gives no training example in this passage. Inference: a winger's conditioning block that adds heavy lower-body strength work and longer threshold-paced intervals, rather than only more aerobic volume, follows the authors' main line.

**Related** — [[claim--vo2max-alone-does-not-determine-endurance-performance]], [[claim--local-blood-flow-not-vo2max-tracks-competition-period-endurance-gains]], [[claim--strength-training-raises-haemoglobin-myoglobin-and-aids-distance-sport]], [[claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]] (Ch1.15, lactate is not a toxin; agreement on a muscle-centred view of lactate), [[case-study--skater-factor-structure-by-qualification]] (the p.253 glycolytic statement), [[framework--strength-endurance-taxonomy-and-absolute-vs-partial]].
=========== heuristic--phasic-biomechanical-analysis-before-selecting-special-strength-means
# Select Special Strength Means from a Phase-by-Phase Analysis of the Sport Movement, Ideally Video Synchronised with Force Data

**What it is** — Under "4.3.6 Correspondence of Training Means to the Sports Movements," the authors say the understanding of muscular work "is derived from analysis of the athlete's movements," most conveniently "a high speed video system to record and analyse each movement at intervals separated by fractions of a second" (PDF pp. 258-259 / printed pp. 247-248). The kinematic structure "helps to identify those actions which play either a fundamental or supportive role in determining motor skill," and knowledge is "more precise if it is based on quantitative information which can be obtained only from computerised video analysis." Analysis can use "the phasic structure of the movement (according to Donskoi)": the act is divided into phases "in which the direction of movement, the application of force and the character of muscular work are distinguished," and the picture "will be more complete if forces are simultaneously recorded along with the video images (e.g. using a force plate or cable tensiometer)." Because "full reproduction of the complex interaction of the different types of fitness strength is not always possible in training," it becomes necessary "to exercise locally the interacting muscle groups that are crucial for controlling specific movements," based on how the kinesiological structure forms (see 2.1.2, 2.1.3). Its elements develop with "heterochronicity" (see 2.2.3): elements interacting directly with external objects develop faster than those interacting indirectly, and "relatively harmonious development of its elements" requires "an organised system of special strength training." The section ends: "success in selecting the means of special strength training is determined by a thorough knowledge of the biomechanics of the movements." (PDF p. 259 / printed p. 248.)

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: the five criteria can only be checked against a movement whose phases, force directions and work regimes are known, and quantitative records make that knowledge precise. They give no evidence that analysed selection outperforms unanalysed selection.

**When to apply** — Before building a special strength menu for a skill: film it at high frame rate, split it into phases, and for each phase note movement direction, force application and type of muscular work; add force-plate data where possible. Then choose local exercises for the muscle groups that control the critical phases. Eric's baseline: "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q6)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 33). Inference: the authors' video-plus-force analysis is the "gather data" step that follows the coach's eye.

**When NOT to apply** — The claim that precise knowledge "can be obtained only from computerised video analysis" is the authors' judgment, not a tested finding, and dates from the book's era of equipment. The heterochronicity point is a cross-reference to Ch2 rather than new evidence. Inference: a full phase analysis is costly; for a team roster it may only be practical for a few key skills.

**Example** — The book gives no worked example in 4.3.6. Inference: a running back's cut could be split into the approach, the plant (eccentric braking), and the push-off (concentric), with a force plate under the plant foot showing the force direction in each phase.

**Related** — [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[framework--kinesiological-pattern-and-strength-field-components]] (Ch2.1.3), [[framework--kinematic-pair-chain-system-movement-analysis-levels]], [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]] (Ch2.2.4), [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/heuristic--emg-timing-shortlists-exercises-it-does-not-prove-transfer]] (Moyer: phase analysis shortlists exercises but does not prove transfer; a caution this section does not state).
=========== case-study--high-jumper-factor-structure-by-qualification
# High Jumpers (Nikitin 1983): As Qualification Rises, Isometric Knee-Extension Power Moves Up and Plantarflexor Power Moves Down the Factor Structure

**What it is** — The authors present factor analysis as a way to study the structure of special physical preparedness, "especially informative" when it compares athletes of different qualification or one athlete at different stages; data from many sports show "distinct changes in the structure of an athlete's physical preparedness with increasing sports proficiency" (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252). Table 4.1 (Nikitin 1983), "The factor structure (in %) of Special Physical Preparedness of high jumpers, in terms of the major factors displayed by a large sample of competitors of different levels of qualification," verified against the page image:

| Factor | Class 2-3 athletes | % | Class 1 - MS | % |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | General athletic preparedness | 29.6 | Specific athletic preparedness | 27.4 |
| II | Power of plantarflexors | 19.6 | Power of knee extension isometrically | 23.4 |
| III | Power of knee extension in dynamic regime | 13.0 | Power of knee extension dynamically | 18.5 |
| IV | Isometric strength of knee extensors | 10.5 | Power of plantarflexors | 11.8 |
| V | Explosive-strength of knee extensors (isometric) | 6.5 | (none listed) | |

The authors' reading: higher-class jumpers develop the specific ability to generate powerful take-off force (factor I) and powerful body extension with the knee and back extensors (factor III); explosive force of the take-off leg's extensors under isometric conditions (factor II) "assumes major significance," growing from what were factors IV and V in Class 2-3; plantarflexor indicators move from factor II to factor IV, "the contribution of which diminishes significantly"; and "the role of special physical preparedness of jumpers increases with level of qualification." (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252.)

**Why it works** — Here the authors do give a mechanism. Isometric strength matters at high level "due to the large loading of the muscles during the take-off, where the support (take-off) leg acts as a lever, and converts into vertical lift the angular velocity acquired during the run-up." Plantarflexors fade "because under intense overloading the muscles of the support leg are already unable to make a significant contribution to the dynamics of the take-off." (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252.)

**When to apply** — For jumpers and athletes whose key action is a planted, high-load take-off: as qualification rises, give more weight to isometric and explosive-isometric knee-extensor strength in the take-off position. Inference: the falling plantarflexor share may justify a smaller plantarflexor emphasis, but the book reports a factor share, not a training reduction. More generally, the authors' rule is to plan from "the general trends of change in the factor structure ... with increase in proficiency, as well as the individual peculiarities of a specific athlete" (PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253). Eric's baseline: isometric mid-thigh pull peak force enters the DSI used to choose between plyometric and max-strength emphasis. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 76). Inference: these data are a reason to keep an isometric knee-extension measure for jumpers, but they say nothing about the DSI ratio itself.

**When NOT to apply** — The sample is described only as "a large sample"; the number, factor-extraction method and test battery are not given. The percentages do not sum to 100 (about 79% for Class 2-3 and 81% for Class 1-MS), and the text does not say what the remainder is. The labels changing between columns ("general" to "specific" athletic preparedness) mean factors are not the same variables across groups, so the shifts are interpretive. This is high-jump data; Inference: transfer to other take-off actions (a cut, a block) is not shown.

**Example** — The book's own: Table 4.1 above.

**Related** — [[case-study--skater-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[framework--four-level-functional-specialisation-and-special-physical-preparedness]], [[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]] (4.2.4, explosive isometrics, which the text cross-references), [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]] (Ch2.2.4; agreement on qualification-dependent order), [[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]] (limits of correlation-based structure studies).

=========== case-study--high-jumper-factor-structure-by-qualification
# High Jumpers (Nikitin 1983): As Qualification Rises, Isometric Knee-Extension Power Moves Up and Plantarflexor Power Moves Down the Factor Structure

**What it is** — The authors present factor analysis as a way to study the structure of special physical preparedness, "especially informative" when it compares athletes of different qualification or one athlete at different stages; data from many sports show "distinct changes in the structure of an athlete's physical preparedness with increasing sports proficiency" (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252). Table 4.1 (Nikitin 1983), "The factor structure (in %) of Special Physical Preparedness of high jumpers, in terms of the major factors displayed by a large sample of competitors of different levels of qualification," verified against the page image:

| Factor | Class 2-3 athletes | % | Class 1 - MS | % |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | General athletic preparedness | 29.6 | Specific athletic preparedness | 27.4 |
| II | Power of plantarflexors | 19.6 | Power of knee extension isometrically | 23.4 |
| III | Power of knee extension in dynamic regime | 13.0 | Power of knee extension dynamically | 18.5 |
| IV | Isometric strength of knee extensors | 10.5 | Power of plantarflexors | 11.8 |
| V | Explosive-strength of knee extensors (isometric) | 6.5 | (none listed) | |

The authors' reading: higher-class jumpers develop the specific ability to generate powerful take-off force (factor I) and powerful body extension with the knee and back extensors (factor III); explosive force of the take-off leg's extensors under isometric conditions (factor II) "assumes major significance," growing from what were factors IV and V in Class 2-3; plantarflexor indicators move from factor II to factor IV, "the contribution of which diminishes significantly"; and "the role of special physical preparedness of jumpers increases with level of qualification." (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252.)

**Why it works** — Here the authors do give a mechanism. Isometric strength matters at high level "due to the large loading of the muscles during the take-off, where the support (take-off) leg acts as a lever, and converts into vertical lift the angular velocity acquired during the run-up." Plantarflexors fade "because under intense overloading the muscles of the support leg are already unable to make a significant contribution to the dynamics of the take-off." (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252.)

**When to apply** — For jumpers and athletes whose key action is a planted, high-load take-off: as qualification rises, give more weight to isometric and explosive-isometric knee-extensor strength in the take-off position. Inference: the falling plantarflexor share may justify a smaller plantarflexor emphasis, but the book reports a factor share, not a training reduction. More generally, the authors' rule is to plan from "the general trends of change in the factor structure ... with increase in proficiency, as well as the individual peculiarities of a specific athlete" (PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253). Eric's baseline: isometric mid-thigh pull peak force enters the DSI used to choose between plyometric and max-strength emphasis. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 76). Inference: these data are a reason to keep an isometric knee-extension measure for jumpers, but they say nothing about the DSI ratio itself.

The percentages do not sum to 100 (about 79% for Class 2-3 and 81% for Class 1-MS), and the text does not say what the remainder is. The labels changing between columns ("general" to "specific" athletic preparedness) mean factors are not the same variables across groups, so the shifts are interpretive. =========== framework--four-level-functional-specialisation-and-special-physical-preparedness
# Functional Specialisation in Four Levels: General Abilities, Coordination, Explosive Force and Specific Endurance, Then the Structure of Special Physical Preparedness

**What it is** — Under "The Process of Functional Specialisation," the authors give "an ascending flowchart" of how the body specialises "over many years of training" (Fig 4.24, verified against the page image; PDF p. 262 / printed p. 251):
- **Level 1 (generalised abilities):** speed, strength and endurance, the "flexible mechanisms of coordination, regulation and energy production" that serve daily life and "offer extensive possibilities for adaptation."
- **Level 2:** coordination. The demands of sport "stimulate the motor function, which coordinates all muscular activity."
- **Level 3:** the ability to display explosive force, and specific endurance. "The motor function specialises chiefly by developing the ability to display explosive force and specific endurance independent of the type of sport." Specific endurance "may be predominantly cardiovascular or local muscular in nature," and explosive force relates to starting strength, acceleration-strength and absolute strength (3.2.1).
- **Level 4 (specialised abilities):** the structure of special physical preparedness, formed in "the intensive stage of functional specialisation," which "displays its own form with respect to interaction of the cardiovascular-respiratory and motor systems."

Within these structures the functional systems relate by **cooperation** ("effective interaction of all the systems") or **subordination** ("the productivity of one system is enhanced by the functional potentials of the others"). "The structure of special physical preparedness is determined by the specific training regime, and does not relate to conditions imposed by other sporting activities. This fact should be noted by anyone who may be contemplating the use of generalised cross training with various sports." (PDF pp. 262-263 / printed pp. 251-252, verified against the page images.)

**Why it works** — The authors present it as a description of the general sequence, not a tested model; the only mechanism given is that sporting demands stimulate the motor function, which then specialises. No data are attached to the flowchart.

**When to apply** — As a long-term development map: build general speed, strength and endurance and coordination first, then explosive force and specific endurance, then the sport's own structure of preparedness. Use the cross-training warning when another sport is proposed as preparation: the authors say it does not build the target sport's special preparedness. Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next)" is the department's programming "compass." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 101). Inference: both are bottom-up hierarchies that end in sport-specific ability; the Vermeil sequence orders physical qualities, while this flowchart puts coordination below explosive force and specific endurance.

**When NOT to apply** — "Independent of the type of sport" at Level 3 and "does not relate to conditions imposed by other sporting activities" at Level 4 pull in different directions: Level 3 is general across sports, Level 4 is not. The text gives no ages, durations or criteria for moving between levels. The cross-training statement is a strong claim without cited data; it addresses special preparedness, not general fitness or recovery uses of other sports.

**Example** — The book gives no worked example for the flowchart; its factor-analysis tables for high jumpers and skaters (see Related) are offered as data on the Level 4 structure.

**Related** — [[case-study--high-jumper-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[case-study--skater-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[principle--motor-system-leads-cardiorespiratory-adaptation-do-not-separate-them]], [[framework--key-specific-nonspecific-levelling-motor-ability-model]] (Ch2.3.4), [[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]] (Ch2.3.1; agreement), [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]] (Ch3.2.1), [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]] (Ch1.5).
=========== claim--strength-training-raises-haemoglobin-myoglobin-and-aids-distance-sport
# The Authors Claim Strength Training Raises Haemoglobin and Myoglobin More Than Endurance Training and Helps Distance Sports More Than Aerobic Training

**What it is** — Under the subheading "Strength Training and General Endurance," the authors cite "research showing that strength training leads to a greater rise in haemoglobin content (Petrov & Lapchenkov, 1978) and myoglobin (Pattengale & Holloszy, 1967; Hemmingsen, 1963) than endurance training; and that strength training, even in the beginning stages of training, contributes more to the largest improvements in distance sports than aerobic training (Neminushchii & Filin, 1972; Gavrilenko & Mikhailov, 1981)" (PDF pp. 261-262 / printed pp. 250-251, verified against the page images). "Several decades ago, scientists pointed out the importance of local (strength) endurance for cyclic types of sport" (seven citations, 1962-1974), "but in our time, it has not been given serious attention," because endurance methods aimed "chiefly at improving the cardiovascular-respiratory functions (mainly by distance training)" (PDF p. 262 / printed p. 251).

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism in this passage. Inference: it follows from their preceding argument that endurance depends on the muscles' strength and oxidative qualities (see Related), but they do not state that link here.

**When to apply** — As a reason to keep strength training in endurance and repeat-effort athletes' programs rather than replacing it with more aerobic volume. Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block." Tagged **Inferred (transcript + slides)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182). Inference: this claim runs the other way from the usual interference concern: here strength is said to help endurance, not endurance to harm strength.

**When NOT to apply** — Why `contested`: one citation does not appear to support the sentence it is attached to. The published title of Pattengale & Holloszy (Am J Physiol 1967;213(3):783-785) is "Augmentation of skeletal muscle myoglobin by a program of treadmill running": a running (endurance) program, not strength training. Only the title and journal listing were checked, not the paper's content, so the book's comparison of strength and endurance training cannot be confirmed from that source. The other citations are Soviet or older, not described in the text, and not in the library. "Contributes more to the largest improvements in distance sports than aerobic training" gives no sport, measure or size of effect. In this library, the Ch1 entry on circuit training and Issurin's concurrent-training case study describe the opposite direction of interaction (endurance work compromising strength), which does not contradict this claim but limits how it combines with endurance volume.

**Example** — The book gives no worked example. Inference: a cross-country runner who adds two heavy strength sessions a week in the base phase, instead of a fourth easy run, is the kind of change this claim argues for.

**Related** — [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]], [[principle--motor-system-leads-cardiorespiratory-adaptation-do-not-separate-them]], [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]] (Ch1.12, endurance work compromising strength), [[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]] (Issurin, interference in the other direction).
=========== heuristic--parachute-resistance-sizing-progression-and-contrast-release
# Parachute Resistance: Choose Parachute Size by the Speed Quality, Progress Over Weeks, and Use the Quick Release as a Contrast Method

**What it is** — Under the heading "Parachute Resistance Training" the authors describe small parachutes of different sizes attached to the trunk with a quick-release harness as "a low-inertia form of resistance" (Popov 1966). They note claims that the parachutes were developed secretly in Moscow in 1988 (Brunner & Tabachnik 1990) and say the Popov reference shows such research "more than 20 years earlier" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243). Their prescription (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244):
- Drag "increases rapidly with velocity (actually the square of the velocity)." The drag force "characteristically varies between 5 - 200 Newtons for running speeds of 6 - 10 metres per second, depending on the size of the parachute (Zatsiorsky, 1995)."
- Size by quality: "smaller parachutes are more suited for speed development, medium parachutes for speed-endurance and large parachutes for speed-strength and acceleration-strength." Since speed sets drag, the athlete should try "to run at maximum speed for as long as possible," using fartlek or interval methods.
- Distances "commonly vary between 30m and 150m, with smaller parachutes being used for the longer distances."
- Quick release at maximum velocity is "a special contrast method in enhancing speed and stride frequency" (also PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243, citing acceleration strength, 7.1).
- Progression: "gradual progressive overloading ... with larger parachutes being used over a period of weeks," with periodic decreases in loading within a workout or microcycle, plus the sudden-release contrast method (see 1.16.3). Within a workout, "it is common to progress rapidly after the warm-up to the use of large resistance parachutes, then conclude with a few repetitions using smaller parachutes."
- To avoid after-effects on normal skill, "precede and follow all parachute sessions with the same exercises performed without parachutes."
- In preparatory weekly microcycles, sessions are "typically" two or three times a week on alternate days, and more frequent "nearer the later stage of the preparatory phase immediately preceding the competitive season."
- Users can include distance runners, sprint or distance cyclists, and swimmers.

The authors add that in the West the parachutes "generally have been applied fairly randomly with little knowledge of periodising them," and that "Appropriateness of use depends on an understanding of which strength qualities are required by the athlete at a given stage of training" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243).

**Why it works** — The authors give the physics: the parachutes' aerodynamic resistance "increases rapidly with velocity (actually the square of the velocity)," which "allows us to use these devices more knowledgeably" and "Naturally, running speed determines the degree of drag resistance" (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244), so parachute size and running speed together set the load. Inference: velocity-squared drag is the textbook drag equation, and this relation is the only part of the entry that could rate `proven`; the size-to-quality mapping, distances, frequencies and progression are the authors' practice recommendations with no cited trial, so the entry as a whole is `supported`. The authors give no mechanism for why the quick-release contrast enhances stride frequency.

**When to apply** — When adding resisted running for speed qualities: pick the parachute size for the quality targeted (small for speed, large for acceleration-strength), keep efforts near maximal speed, bracket the parachute runs with unresisted runs of the same drill, and place the sessions in the later preparatory phase. Eric's baseline: speed residuals drive programming: "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q16)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 97). Inference: the authors' "more frequently nearer the later stage of the preparatory phase" fits an off-season speed block that ends close to camp, but the book gives no in-season guidance for parachutes.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors say parachute training "plays no role in the development of starting strength" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243), so it is not a starting-strength tool. They warn it can disrupt skill and correspondence (see [[claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence]]). The 5-200 N range is a secondary citation (Zatsiorsky 1995) without the parachute sizes that produce each value, so it cannot be used to choose a specific parachute. No frequency, distance or progression figure here comes from a reported controlled study.

**Example** — The book's own: within a workout, progress quickly after the warm-up to a large parachute, then finish with a few runs on a smaller parachute, with unresisted runs of the same exercise before and after (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244).

**Related** — [[claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence]], [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[framework--strength-speed-continuum-five-zones]], [[research-papers/petrakos-2016-resisted-sled-sprint-training-to-improve-sprint-performance-a-systematic-review]] (sled rather than parachute; the modern resisted-sprint evidence in the vault).
=========== claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence
# Parachutes Avoid Extra Vertical Loading, but Resist the Flight Phase and Alter Landing Positions, Reducing Dynamic Correspondence

**What it is** — The authors give one advantage and several limits of parachute resistance.
- Advantage: parachutes "offer a safer alternative to the use of weights added to the extremities or body, or dragged behind the athlete (e.g. a car tyre or sled), because they do not increase the vertical reaction forces acting on the body" (PDF pp. 254-255 / printed pp. 243-244).
- Limit 1: "parachutes offer the same degree of resistance during both the support and non-support phases of running, thereby disrupting speed and acceleration of limb and body movement during flight."
- Limit 2: "parachutes alter the relative position of the joints during landing, especially during hurdling and jumping."
- Together: "All of this can adversely affect several aspects of the degree of dynamic correspondence of the training means to the actual sporting movements (as discussed throughout Ch 4.3)." (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244.)
- Scope: parachute training "plays no role in the development of starting strength, which is produced under isometric conditions" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243).

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasons are mechanical: no added mass means no extra vertical reaction force, while a drag force acting through the whole stride also acts in flight, where the sport has no external resistance. They give no data on injury rates for parachutes against sleds or limb weights. Inference: the safety claim rests on the vertical-force argument alone.

**When to apply** — When choosing between parachute, sled and worn-weight resistance: if vertical loading is the concern, the authors' argument favours the parachute (Inference: for example, heavy athletes or athletes returning from lower-limb injury; the book names no population); if preserving flight-phase and landing mechanics is the concern (the book names hurdlers and jumpers), it counts against it. Eric's baseline: Dynamic Correspondence governs "whether an exercise actually transfers." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 103). Inference: a coach weighing a parachute block can use these two limits as the checklist for what to watch on film.

**When NOT to apply** — The safety advantage is asserted, not measured, in the text; the book cites no comparison of injury or tissue loading. The sled is named only in the safety sentence, and the book does not compare sled and parachute on dynamic correspondence. Inference: modern sled studies (see Related) address performance, not this book's safety claim, so they neither confirm nor refute it.

**Example** — The book's own: hurdlers and jumpers whose joint positions at landing are altered by the parachute (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244).

**Related** — [[heuristic--parachute-resistance-sizing-progression-and-contrast-release]], [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[heuristic--match-amplitude-direction-and-line-of-resistance-to-the-sport]] (the weighted-belt example: vertical loading trains anti-gravity muscles), [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--wearable-resistance-kinetic-energy-sprint]] (limb-worn resistance, which the authors call less safe), [[research-papers/petrakos-2016-resisted-sled-sprint-training-to-improve-sprint-performance-a-systematic-review]].

- Progression: "gradual progressive overloading ... with larger parachutes being used over a period of weeks," with periodic decreases in loading within a workout or microcycle, plus the sudden-release contrast method (see 1.16.3). Within a workout, "it is common to progress rapidly after the warm-up to the use of large resistance parachutes, then conclude with a few repetitions using smaller parachutes."
- To avoid after-effects on normal skill, "precede and follow all parachute sessions with the same exercises performed without parachutes."
- In preparatory weekly microcycles, sessions are "typically" two or three times a week on alternate days, and more frequent "nearer the later stage of the preparatory phase immediately preceding the competitive season."
- Users can include distance runners, sprint or distance cyclists, and swimmers.

The authors add that in the West the parachutes "generally have been applied fairly randomly with little knowledge of periodising them," and that "Appropriateness of use depends on an understanding of which strength qualities are required by the athlete at a given stage of training" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243).

**Why it works** — The authors give the physics: the parachutes' aerodynamic resistance "increases rapidly with velocity (actually the square of the velocity)," which "allows us to use these devices more knowledgeably" and "Naturally, running speed determines the degree of drag resistance" (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244), so parachute size and running speed together set the load. Inference: velocity-squared drag is the textbook drag equation, and this relation is the only part of the entry that could rate `proven`; the size-to-quality mapping, distances, frequencies and progression are the authors' practice recommendations with no cited trial, so the entry as a whole is `supported`. The authors give no mechanism for why the quick-release contrast enhances stride frequency.

**When to apply** — When adding resisted running for speed qualities: pick the parachute size for the quality targeted (small for speed, large for acceleration-strength), keep efforts near maximal speed, bracket the parachute runs with unresisted runs of the same drill, and place the sessions in the later preparatory phase. Eric's baseline: speed residuals drive programming: "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q16)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 97). Inference: the authors' "more frequently nearer the later stage of the preparatory phase" fits an off-season speed block that ends close to camp, but the book gives no in-season guidance for parachutes.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors say parachute training "plays no role in the development of starting strength" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243), so it is not a starting-strength tool. They warn it can disrupt skill and correspondence (see [[claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence]]). The 5-200 N range is a secondary citation (Zatsiorsky 1995) without the parachute sizes that produce each value, so it cannot be used to choose a specific parachute. No frequency, distance or progression figure here comes from a reported controlled study.

**Example** — The book's own: within a workout, progress quickly after the warm-up to a large parachute, then finish with a few runs on a smaller parachute, with unresisted runs of the same exercise before and after (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244).

**Related** — [[claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence]], [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[framework--strength-speed-continuum-five-zones]], [[research-papers/petrakos-2016-resisted-sled-sprint-training-to-improve-sprint-performance-a-systematic-review]] (sled rather than parachute; the modern resisted-sprint evidence in the vault).
=========== claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence
# Parachutes Avoid Extra Vertical Loading, but Resist the Flight Phase and Alter Landing Positions, Reducing Dynamic Correspondence

**What it is** — The authors give one advantage and several limits of parachute resistance.
- Advantage: parachutes "offer a safer alternative to the use of weights added to the extremities or body, or dragged behind the athlete (e.g. a car tyre or sled), because they do not increase the vertical reaction forces acting on the body" (PDF pp. 254-255 / printed pp. 243-244).
- Limit 1: "parachutes offer the same degree of resistance during both the support and non-support phases of running, thereby disrupting speed and acceleration of limb and body movement during flight."
- Limit 2: "parachutes alter the relative position of the joints during landing, especially during hurdling and jumping."
- Together: "All of this can adversely affect several aspects of the degree of dynamic correspondence of the training means to the actual sporting movements (as discussed throughout Ch 4.3)." (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244.)
- Scope: parachute training "plays no role in the development of starting strength, which is produced under isometric conditions" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243).

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasons are mechanical: no added mass means no extra vertical reaction force, while a drag force acting through the whole stride also acts in flight, where the sport has no external resistance. They give no data on injury rates for parachutes against sleds or limb weights. Inference: the safety claim rests on the vertical-force argument alone.

**When to apply** — When choosing between parachute, sled and worn-weight resistance: if vertical loading is the concern, the authors' argument favours the parachute (Inference: for example, heavy athletes or athletes returning from lower-limb injury; the book names no population); if preserving flight-phase and landing mechanics is the concern (the book names hurdlers and jumpers), it counts against it. Eric's baseline: Dynamic Correspondence governs "whether an exercise actually transfers." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 103). Inference: a coach weighing a parachute block can use these two limits as the checklist for what to watch on film.

**When NOT to apply** — The safety advantage is asserted, not measured, in the text; the book cites no comparison of injury or tissue loading. The sled is named only in the safety sentence, and the book does not compare sled and parachute on dynamic correspondence. Inference: modern sled studies (see Related) address performance, not this book's safety claim, so they neither confirm nor refute it.

**Example** — The book's own: hurdlers and jumpers whose joint positions at landing are altered by the parachute (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244).

**Related** — [[heuristic--parachute-resistance-sizing-progression-and-contrast-release]], [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[heuristic--match-amplitude-direction-and-line-of-resistance-to-the-sport]] (the weighted-belt example: vertical loading trains anti-gravity muscles), [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--wearable-resistance-kinetic-energy-sprint]] (limb-worn resistance, which the authors call less safe), [[research-papers/petrakos-2016-resisted-sled-sprint-training-to-improve-sprint-performance-a-systematic-review]].

# Evans's Worked Example: Applying the Five Dynamic-Correspondence Criteria to a Wrestling Clinch Takedown

**What it is** — After presenting the standard five Dynamic Correspondence criteria
(amplitude/direction of movement, accentuated region of force production, dynamics of effort,
rate and time of maximum force production, regime of muscular work - the same five-factor
list Eric's baseline independently records as course material; Eric's baseline:
`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing the Principle of Dynamic Correspondence,
Verkhoshansky), Evans's slides (U2 L4 p.21-22) work through a specific technique: "Takedown
from a clinch that is executed from the position of having low double under hooks secured
against the lower back of the opponent." His analysis, quoted directly: amplitude/direction -
"Lifting the opponent begins in an upward rotational fashion that allows the hips to
transition for the downward rotational movement during the throw towards the mat... The
amplitude of hip and back extension is rather small as the lift is initiated from a
relatively upright posture to begin with while the subsequent rotational element is more
pronounced"; region of force production - "The point in which the greatest forces are
generated is when the hips and back are nearly fully extended as you take balance away from
your opponent by lifting him or her partially or completely off the mat"; dynamics of effort -
"one considers the biomechanical positions associated with the takedown to include your
underhook technique, posture, proximity of your hips to your opponents, leg position,
etcetera both during the initiation of the throw as well as during the throw"; rate and time
of force production - "the lift/throw is where the greatest speed is generated and the time
of execution may be quantified, albeit in a rudimentary fashion, via a coach with a stop
watch who estimates the distance over which the movement is performed... arrives at a
workable figure for rate and time"; regime of muscular work - the initial hip control to
immobilize the opponent is "an isometric, or sustaining, muscle effort," while the subsequent
throw "consists of dynamic (moving) and ballistic (explosive) muscle effort."

**Why it works** — Evans does not state a mechanism for why walking through these five
criteria on a specific technique improves exercise selection beyond the general Dynamic
Correspondence premise (shared movement amplitude, force region, effort dynamics, force
timing, and muscular-work regime should predict better transfer, a premise this course does
not re-derive but assumes from the earlier slides). Inference: the value of this example is
methodological, not mechanistic - it demonstrates how a coach without laboratory equipment can
still apply the five criteria qualitatively (his own phrase, "albeit in a rudimentary
fashion... via a coach with a stop watch") to a single competitive technique, rather than only
to whole sports in the abstract.

**When to apply** — As a template for walking a coach through the same five-question audit on
any single competitive skill (a football block, a tackle, a route break) when selecting
weight-room exercises intended to transfer to it. Eric's baseline: HHPR 5355 teaches this
same five-factor Dynamic Correspondence model in the abstract but does not record a worked
single-technique example in the transcript material reviewed for the baseline
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power"). Inference: this Evans example fills that
specific gap with a concrete, if combat-sport-specific, illustration of the method.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single illustrative example on a wrestling
technique, not a validated case study with measured data; Evans supplies no actual timing,
force, or EMG data for this takedown, only a qualitative walk-through, and he explicitly
concedes the timing method he describes ("void of accounting precisely for the curvilinear
pattern") is approximate. Do not treat this as evidence that the five-criteria method
produces accurate or reliable exercise-selection decisions; it demonstrates the method's
steps, not its validity. It is also sport-specific to wrestling's clinch takedown; applying
the same five questions to a different sport's skill (e.g., a football pass-rush move) would
require a new, separate qualitative analysis, not a direct transfer of this one's conclusions.
Confidence is untested.

**Example** — The wrestling clinch takedown itself, described above, is the example.

**Related** — Reciprocal-link suggestion: `supertraining--verkhoshansky` likely stages
Verkhoshansky's own statement of the Dynamic Correspondence criteria (the entry writer did
not locate an exact-title match during this ingest's dedup grep, which returned
`principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions.md` as the closest candidate); a reviewer
should compare that entry's dimension count and wording against the five-factor version used
here and in Eric's baseline, and link them if they describe the same underlying model at
different levels of detail.
</content>

=========== claim--isometric-regional-specificity-not-strictly-angular
**What it is** — Many studies report isometric training producing maximum strength gains at
or very close to the trained joint angle, leading some athletes to avoid isometric training
altogether; the authors argue this "angular specificity" framing needs critical revision,
citing other studies showing isometric training also produces significant strength increase
up to about 15 degrees either side of the training angle. Because every type of muscle
contraction has its own force/torque-versus-joint-angle curve (see 2.1.2), the authors argue
it is "highly unlikely" that strength gain would be confined to one precise angle and
nowhere else, and prefer the term "regional specificity" over "angular specificity" (or
muscle-length specificity). Thepault-Mathieu et al (1988) found this regional specificity is
strongest when the muscle trains in its most shortened position and weakest when it trains
most lengthened: males training isometrically for 5 weeks (5 sets of 5 reps, 5 seconds each,
